lead: A cockpit is the crew's office. In an analog cockpit, each quantity gets its own dial, moved by a sensor through wires or mechanical linkages. In a glass cockpit, a few screens replace many dials. Computers draw pages on those screens from the same sensor data. The change raises information density: the crew sees more useful data in less space. It also adds dependence on power, cooling and software. Civil airliners, military transports and business jets all use glass today; older aircraft remain analog or hybrid.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.2 on avionics architecture, IMA and LRUs, because displays are fed by the architecture.

sections.h3: Analog cockpit: one dial per job

blocks.text: An analog cockpit uses direct-reading dials. A dial is a round instrument with a pointer. The pointer moves because a sensor sends a signal, or because a mechanical linkage turns it. The airspeed indicator, altimeter, vertical speed indicator, attitude indicator, heading indicator, engine tachometer and fuel gauge each have their own case and their own place on the panel.

items: Each dial is single-function: it shows one quantity and nothing else.
Wiring is point-to-point: a sensor wire goes to its dial, not to a shared network.
Warnings are dedicated: a red lamp, a horn or a stick shaker for one condition.
Part count is high: many dials, many connectors, many lamps.
Mechanical linkages are common in older aircraft: cables, rods and pulleys move pointers or control surfaces.

blocks.text: The analog cockpit is robust in a simple way. A failed dial does not blank the others. A dial with a direct mechanical link can still read after an electrical failure. The cost is space and crew workload. Twenty or more dials spread across the panel, and the crew must scan them one by one. Adding a new function means adding another instrument.

sections.h3: Glass cockpit: fewer screens, more pages

blocks.text: A glass cockpit replaces most dials with electronic displays. Early glass used cathode-ray tubes (CRTs); modern glass uses liquid-crystal displays (LCDs). A display is a screen, not a sensor. It receives digital data from a symbol generator. The symbol generator is a computer that turns sensor and system data into pixels: lines, scales, numbers and colours.

blocks.where: N_slots is the total number of page slots available across displays; D is the number of displays; P is the number of pages each display can show at different times. A page slot is one display showing one selected page. Displays may share the same page definitions, so the number of distinct pages can be smaller than N_slots.

items: Sensors measure air data, attitude, engine and system values.
The symbol generator receives those values over data buses.
The generator draws the selected page on the selected display.
The crew changes pages with a control panel or a cursor.
A central warning computer collects failures and shows them on a shared warning page.

blocks.text: A page is a screen layout. One page can contain several dial functions: a primary flight page might show airspeed, attitude, altitude and heading together. One display can show a primary flight display page, then a navigation page, then an engine page. The same display is reconfigurable: it is not tied to one quantity. Page count and function count are separate counts. Four displays with six pages each give 4 × 6 = 24 page slots over time, while 24 dial functions split evenly need six functions per display at once, arranged on one or more pages.

A hybrid cockpit sits between the two. It keeps some analog dials and adds one or two CRT or LCD screens. Many older airliners were upgraded this way: the centre panel got a screen, while the primary dials stayed. A hybrid is not a failed glass cockpit; it is a deliberate mix chosen for cost, certification or training.

sections.h3: Why glass needs power, cooling and software assurance

blocks.text: Glass improves information density but moves the failure points. A dial needs a sensor and a wire. A glass display needs a sensor, a data bus, a symbol generator, a display, electrical power and cooling. If power is lost, several screens can go blank together. If cooling fails, an LCD can overheat and dim or shut down. If software has a defect, a page can show a wrong scale or a stale value.

items: Power: displays and symbol generators draw electrical power; emergency power must keep the essential pages alive.
Cooling: CRT and LCD displays produce heat; avionics bays need airflow or liquid cooling.
Software assurance: the symbol generator is software-controlled; its development follows a software assurance standard such as DO-178B (DO-178C for newer designs).
Data validity: a display is only as good as its sensor and bus data; a valid-looking page can still be wrong.

blocks.text: The trap is the phrase 'glass cockpit'. It does not mean paperless, and it does not mean sensorless. The screens still need valid sensor data and a working symbol generator. The crew still needs checklists, and the aircraft still needs air data probes, gyros or inertial sensors, and engine sensors. The display is the last step in a chain, not the whole chain. For the page formats themselves, see Chapter 4.4.

examples.question: An analog cockpit has 24 dials. A glass cockpit uses 4 displays, and each display can show up to 6 pages at different times. How many page slots are available? If the 24 dial functions are split evenly across the 4 displays and all must be available at the same time, how many dial functions must each display present at once?
steps: Page slots = number of displays × pages per display = 4 × 6 = 24 page slots.
Dial functions to replace = 24 dial functions.
Functions per display at once = 24 dial functions ÷ 4 displays = 6 functions per display. These six functions can be arranged on one page or spread across pages.
examples.answer: The glass cockpit has 24 page slots. Each display must present 6 dial functions at once if the 24 functions are split evenly. Page slots and dial functions are separate counts.
examples.check:
displays = 4
pages_per_display = 6
dials = 24
page_slots = displays * pages_per_display
functions_per_display = dials // displays
print(page_slots)
print(functions_per_display)

traps: Glass cockpit does not mean paperless or sensorless. Each display still needs valid sensor data and a working symbol generator.
A page is not a new sensor. Reconfiguring a display changes the drawing, not the measured quantity.

Do not count page slots and dial functions as the same. Four displays with six pages each give 24 page slots over time, but only four pages are visible at once. The 24 dial functions are a separate count; each display can present several functions on one page or across pages.
A hybrid cockpit is a deliberate mix, not necessarily a failure or an incomplete upgrade.
Power loss can blank several glass displays together; a direct-reading analog dial may survive an electrical failure. Compare failure modes, not just normal operation.

quiz.q: Name the two display technologies used in glass cockpits.
quiz.a: Cathode-ray tubes (CRTs) in early glass cockpits and liquid-crystal displays (LCDs) in modern ones.
A cockpit that keeps some analog dials and adds one or more electronic displays.

quiz.q: Why does an analog cockpit have a high part count?
quiz.a: Each quantity needs its own dial, its own wiring or linkage, and often its own warning lamp. Adding a function adds another instrument.

quiz.q: Why does a glass cockpit need cooling?
quiz.a: Displays and symbol generators produce heat. Without cooling, LCDs can overheat and dim or shut down, and electronics can fail.

quiz.q: A glass cockpit has 3 displays, and each display can show 7 pages at different times. It replaces 21 dial functions. How many page slots are available? If the 21 functions are split evenly across the 3 displays and all must be available at once, how many functions must each display present at a time?
quiz.a: Page slots = 3 × 7 = 21. Functions per display at once = 21 ÷ 3 = 7. Page slots and functions are separate counts; the seven functions per display can be arranged on one or more pages.

quiz.q: A display shows a valid-looking airspeed page, but the airspeed number is frozen. Is the glass cockpit automatically safe? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The display only draws data from a sensor and symbol generator. A frozen number means the data chain is faulty. The crew must cross-check with another source and treat the page as invalid.

quiz.q: Compare a single analog dial failure with a single glass display failure in a four-display cockpit.
quiz.a: An analog dial failure loses one quantity. A glass display failure loses every page on that display, but other displays can be reconfigured. The glass failure is wider per screen, so reversion and page priority matter.

beyond: Not for the exam. Newer cockpits add large touchscreens, voice input and head-up or helmet-mounted displays, so the display is becoming one part of a larger human-machine interface. Certification now looks beyond DO-178B to DO-178C and DO-254 for complex hardware. Cyber security of avionics data buses and display computers is an active research area. Search for 'integrated modular avionics display', 'DO-178C', 'touchscreen cockpit certification' and 'avionics cyber security'.
